title: How to Calm Down your Non-Technical stakeholders in under 5 minutes
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni offers technical professionals a short method for defusing angry, confused stakeholders: do not defend yourself, let them talk, then acknowledge and commit to a follow-up. Drawing on her own experiences with a chronic complainer, a senior leader thinking aloud, and a frustrated executive lost in an Excel workbook, she shows that defensiveness and premature logic escalate emotion. She stresses listening as relationship management and timing what you say to when the other person can hear it. She provides concrete phrases such as acknowledging concerns and promising a time frame for a reply. The central move is to let emotion flow first and only then get down to business.
points: Defensiveness fuels stakeholder anger, so the first move is to let them finish and not commit to changes on the spot.
People thinking out loud are not issuing decisions, and interrupting them to solve the problem loses the context you need.
Logic and facts will not land while someone is angry; frustration usually subsides in under five minutes if you listen.
Short acknowledging phrases and a firm follow-up time give frustrated stakeholders a sense of being heard without conceding.
Giving upfront direction, such as a demo, prevents confusion from turning into frustration with non-technical users.
quotes: Research indicates that anger elevates physiological arousal and disrupts neural activity in regions critical for cognitive processing, impairing the brain's ability to make rational decisions. In his fit of rage, his feedback was not rational.

Next time, I let him talk and then took time to filter through what made sense to change or not. I did not commit to changing anything while on the call with him; I just acknowledged I was rotating. This is truthful.

Let someone finish their thought. You need it to have the full context. This interruption might come back to bite you. Whether their out-loud thoughts are logical, you must get to the root of their feelings before taking rational action. This will determine how you later present the logical action that was taken.
Listening is a key part of better relationship management. It shows empathy, which is a win for building trust with your stakeholders.

You see, people will not listen to you, no matter how logical or factual, if they are pissed off. Frustration does not have to last long. Generally, it can be quieted in under 5 minutes if you let them talk. Suppose you are trying to connect with logic while in this state, which will frustrate them more and lengthen the already miserable conversation.
I know I like to lead with facts and rational statements. You can't do that in this situation. Let the emotions flow first, then get down to business.
